claim: Antibody-based immune checkpoint inhibitor drugs are capable of providing a significant percentage of cancer patients with durable anti-tumor responses and improving survival rates compared to traditional standard of care therapies.
source: The antibody-based immune checkpoint inhibitor drugs are likely to remain one of the most effective platforms for IO drug development for the foreseeable future, given that they are capable of providing a significant percentage of cancer patients with durable anti-tumor responses; thus, improving survival rates compared to those treated with traditional standard of care therapies (Ribas and Wolchok, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ribas and Wolchok, 2018

claim: The response rate to IO therapy varies widely among tumor types, ranging from 15% objective response rate for Head and Neck cancer to 87% objective response rate for Hodgkin's Disease.
source: However, the response rate to IO therapy varies widely among tumor types - ranging from a low of 15% objective response rate for Head and Neck cancer patients to a high of 87% objective response rate for patients with Hodgkin's Disease (Ribas and Wolchok, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ribas and Wolchok, 2018

claim: There is a need to identify biomarkers capable of predicting which type of cancer or which biomarker sub-stratums would respond best to IO therapy.
source: The lack of broad therapeutic efficacy highlights the need to identify biomarkers capable of predicting either which type of cancer or which biomarker sub-stratums would respond best to the therapy (Chen and Mellman, 2017; Havel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen and Mellman, 2017 and Havel et al., 2019

claim: There is a need to develop other immune checkpoints such as TIM-3, LAG-3, VISTA, CEACAM1 and TIGIT to broaden the scope of therapeutic coverage.
source: In addition, there is a need to develop other immune checkpoints such as TIM-3 (Das et al., 2017; Joller and Kuchroo, 2017), LAG-3 (Anderson et al., 2016; Maruhashi et al., 2018), VISTA (ElTanbouly et al., 2020), CEACAM1 (Khairnar et al., 2018; Dankner et al., 2017) and TIGIT (Manieri et al., 2017; Dougall et al., 2017) to broaden the scope of therapeutic coverage by the current repertoire of checkpoint inhibitor drugs (Le Mercier et al., 2015; Marhelava et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: Several small molecule kinase inhibitors that block specific pathways involved in the regulation of tumor immunity have been proposed.
source: Several small molecule kinase inhibitors that block specific pathways involved in the regulation of tumor immunity have been proposed (Adams et al., 2015; Weinmann, 2016; Sasikumar and Ramachandra, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adams et al., 2015; Weinmann, 2016; Sasikumar and Ramachandra, 2018

claim: The development of small molecule kinase inhibitor drugs relies on mature technologies with a decades-long proven track record of success.
source: The advantage of this approach is the fact that the development of these drugs relies on the use of mature technologies that have a decades-long proven track record of success.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of drug development technologies

claim: Large commercial and proprietary libraries of small molecule compounds exist and the process of high throughput screening to identify specific kinase inhibitors is well-developed.
source: Large commercial and proprietary libraries of small molecule compounds exist and the process of high throughput screening to identify specific kinase inhibitors is well-developed.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of pharmaceutical industry capabilities

claim: There are more than 500 kinases in the human genome.
source: The challenge of using this approach to develop new IO drugs lies in determining which of the more than 500 kinases in the human genome would be appropriate targets (Manning, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manning, 2002

claim: The cancer-immunity cycle is a term used to describe an intricate, multi-step process involving interactions between T cells, other immune cells, cancer cells and epithelial cells throughout the initiation and execution phases of anti-cancer immune responses.
source: The cancer-immunity cycle is a term used to describe an intricate, multi-step process involving interactions between T cells, other immune cells, cancer cells and epithelial cells throughout the initiation and execution phases of anti-cancer immune responses (Chen and Mellman, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen and Mellman, 2013

claim: HPK1, also known as MAP4K1, is a hematopoietic cell-restricted member of the Ste20 family of serine/threonine kinases.
source: HPK1, also known as MAP4K1, is a hematopoietic cell-restricted member of the Ste20 family of serine/threonine kinases that functions as a negative regulator of activation signals generated by the TCR (Kiefer et al., 1996; Hu et al., 1996; Liou et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kiefer et al., 1996; Hu et al., 1996; Liou et al., 2000

claim: HPK1 functions as a negative regulator of activation signals generated by the TCR.
source: HPK1, also known as MAP4K1, is a hematopoietic cell-restricted member of the Ste20 family of serine/threonine kinases that functions as a negative regulator of activation signals generated by the TCR (Kiefer et al., 1996; Hu et al., 1996; Liou et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kiefer et al., 1996; Hu et al., 1996; Liou et al., 2000

claim: HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by the TCR.

evidence: Supported by citation to Liou et al., 2000

claim: HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by BCR.
source: Cell biological studies reveal that HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by a variety of cell surface receptors that are present on many sub-types of hematopoietic cells, including: the TCR (Liou et al., 2000), BCR (Liou et al., 2000; Sauer et al., 2001; Tsuji et al., 2001; Han et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Liou et al., 2000; Sauer et al., 2001; Tsuji et al., 2001; Han et al., 2003

claim: HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by Fas.
source: Cell biological studies reveal that HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by a variety of cell surface receptors that are present on many sub-types of hematopoietic cells, including: the TCR (Liou et al., 2000), BCR (Liou et al., 2000; Sauer et al., 2001; Tsuji et al., 2001; Han et al., 2003), Fas (Chen et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 1999

claim: HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by EPOR.
source: Cell biological studies reveal that HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by a variety of cell surface receptors that are present on many sub-types of hematopoietic cells, including: the TCR (Liou et al., 2000), BCR (Liou et al., 2000; Sauer et al., 2001; Tsuji et al., 2001; Han et al., 2003), Fas (Chen et al., 1999), EPOR (Nagata et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to Nagata et al., 1999

claim: HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by TGFβR.
source: Cell biological studies reveal that HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by a variety of cell surface receptors that are present on many sub-types of hematopoietic cells, including: the TCR (Liou et al., 2000), BCR (Liou et al., 2000; Sauer et al., 2001; Tsuji et al., 2001; Han et al., 2003), Fas (Chen et al., 1999), EPOR (Nagata et al., 1999), TGFβR (Wang et al., 1997; Zhou et al., 1999)

claim: HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by PGE2's EP2R and EP4R.
source: Cell biological studies reveal that HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by a variety of cell surface receptors that are present on many sub-types of hematopoietic cells, including: the TCR (Liou et al., 2000), BCR (Liou et al., 2000; Sauer et al., 2001; Tsuji et al., 2001; Han et al., 2003), Fas (Chen et al., 1999), EPOR (Nagata et al., 1999), TGFβR (Wang et al., 1997; Zhou et al., 1999), PGE2's EP2R and EP4R (Sawasdikosol et al., 2003; Sawasdikosol et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Sawasdikosol et al., 2003; Sawasdikosol et al., 2007

claim: HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by LPS receptors, presumably via TLR2 or TLR4.
source: Cell biological studies reveal that HPK1 is catalytically responsive to activation signals generated by a variety of cell surface receptors that are present on many sub-types of hematopoietic cells, including: the TCR (Liou et al., 2000), BCR (Liou et al., 2000; Sauer et al., 2001; Tsuji et al., 2001; Han et al., 2003), Fas (Chen et al., 1999), EPOR (Nagata et al., 1999), TGFβR (Wang et al., 1997; Zhou et al., 1999), PGE2's EP2R and EP4R (Sawasdikosol et al., 2003; Sawasdikosol et al., 2007) and LPS receptors, presumably via TLR2 or TLR4 (Alzabin et al., 2009).

claim: Upon TCR engagement, HPK1 is recruited to the cholesterol- and sphingomyelin-rich lipid raft microdomain via interactions with LAT and Gads.
source: Upon TCR engagement, HPK1 is recruited to the cholesterol- and sphingomyelin-rich lipid raft microdomain via the interactions with LAT, and Gads (Liou et al., 2000; Ling et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liou et al., 2000; Ling et al., 2001

claim: Once complexed with LAT, HPK1 is phosphorylated on tyrosine 379 by ZAP-70, creating the high affinity binding site for the SH2 domain of SLP-76.
source: Once complexed with LAT, HPK1 is phosphorylated on tyrosine 379 by ZAP-70, creating the high affinity binding site for the SH2 domain of SLP-76.
evidence: Inferred from the description of TCR-mediated HPK1 activation mechanism

claim: The interaction between HPK1 and SLP-76, along with autophosphorylation of HPK1 at threonine 165 and PKD-mediated phosphorylation at serine 171, are required for HPK1 to achieve full catalytic activity.
source: This interaction between HPK1 and SLP-76, along with the autophosphorylation of HPK1 at residue threonine 165 and at a PKD-mediated phosphorylation site at serine 171, are required for HPK1 to achieve full catalytic activity (Sauer et al., 2001; Arnold et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sauer et al., 2001; Arnold et al., 2005

claim: Once catalytically active, HPK1 phosphorylates SLP-76 at serine residue 376 and Gads at threonine residue 262.
source: Once HPK1 becomes catalytically active, HPK1 carries out its role as a negative regulator of TCR-induced signal transduction by phosphorylating SLP-76 at serine residue 376 and Gads at threonine residue 262 (Di Bartolo et al., 2007; Lasserre et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Bartolo et al., 2007; Lasserre et al., 2011

claim: The phosphorylated residues on SLP-76 and Gads form consensus phosphorylation-dependent binding sites for 14-3-3.
source: These phosphorylated residues form consensus phosphorylation-dependent binding sites for 14-3-3 for each of these LAT signalosome members.
evidence: Inferred from the description of HPK1-mediated negative regulation mechanism

claim: The association between phosphorylated SLP-76 and 14-3-3 destabilizes the interaction between SLP-76 and the LAT signalosome.
source: The association between phosphorylated SLP-76 and 14-3-3 destabilizes the interaction between SLP-76 and the LAT signalosome (Di Bartolo et al., 2007; Lasserre et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Bartolo et al., 2007; Lasserre et al., 2011

claim: The dissociated SLP-76 undergoes phosphorylation-dependent ubiquitination at lysine 30 residue, leading to its subsequent proteasome-mediated proteolysis.
source: The dissociated SLP-76 then undergoes phosphorylation-dependent ubiquitination at its lysine 30 residue, leading to its subsequent proteasome-mediated proteolysis (Wang et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012a

claim: HPK1 serves as a negative feedback loop that limits the strength and duration of TCR signals by disrupting the SLP-76/LAT signalosomes.
source: In this model, HPK1 serves as one of the negative feedback loops that limits the strength and duration of TCR signals by disrupting the SLP-76/LAT signalosomes.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanistic description of HPK1 function

claim: HPK1 functions as a negative regulator of BCR-induced B cell activation.
source: HPK1 also functions as a negative regulator of BCR-induced B cell activation, as evidenced by the elevated response profile of ERK, p38, JNK MAPK, PLCγ1, calcium signaling and IKK signaling upon BCR engagement in HPK1-/- B cells (Wang et al., 2012b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012b with data from HPK1-/- B cells

claim: HPK1-/- B cells exhibit elevated levels of ERK, p38, JNK MAPK, PLCγ1, calcium signaling and IKK signaling upon BCR engagement.
source: HPK1 also functions as a negative regulator of BCR-induced B cell activation, as evidenced by the elevated response profile of ERK, p38, JNK MAPK, PLCγ1, calcium signaling and IKK signaling upon BCR engagement in HPK1-/- B cells (Wang et al., 2012b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Wang et al., 2012b

claim: BCR engages Syk and Lyn tyrosine kinases to activate HPK1, presumably via phosphorylation of tyrosine residue 379.
source: The mechanisms used by BCR to activate HPK1 is nearly identical to the one used by TCR. BCR engages Syk and Lyn tyrosine kinases to activate HPK1, presumably via phosphorylation of tyrosine residue 379, which creates the activation-dependent association between tyrosine phosphorylated HPK1 and the SH2 domain of BLNK (Sauer et al., 2001; Tsuji et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sauer et al., 2001; Tsuji et al., 2001 with speculation about mechanism

claim: The phosphorylation of BLNK's threonine residue 152 creates the docking site for 14-3-3 and induces ubiquitination at Lys37, Lys-38, and Lys-40 of BLNK, leading to the subsequent degradation of BLNK.
source: The phosphorylation of BLNK's threonine residue 152 creates the docking site for 14-3-3 and induces ubiquitination at Lys37, Lys-38, and Lys-40 of BLNK, leading to the subsequent degradation of BLNK and the dampening of BLNK-dependent BCR activation signals (Wang et al., 2012b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012b

claim: The catalytic activity of HPK1 is responsive to signals generated by the binding of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) to EP2 and EP4 receptors on T cells.
source: The catalytic activity of HPK1 is responsive to the signals generated by the binding of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) to the rhodopsin-type G protein–coupled receptors, E-prostanoid receptor 2 (EP2) and 4 (EP4) that are present on T cells (Sawasdikosol et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sawasdikosol et al., 2003

claim: PGE2 is the primary eicosanoid product generated when cyclooxygenase 2 (COX-2) catalyzes the conversion of arachidonic acid into PGE2.
source: PGE2 is the primary eicosanoid product generated when cyclooxygenase 2 (COX-2) catalyzes the conversion of arachidonic acid into PGE2 – a pluripotent pro-inflammatory lipid mediator capable of inhibiting TCR-induced T cell activation (Vercammen and Ceuppens, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vercammen and Ceuppens, 1987

claim: PGE2 is a pluripotent pro-inflammatory lipid mediator capable of inhibiting TCR-induced T cell activation.
source: PGE2 is the primary eicosanoid product generated when cyclooxygenase 2 (COX-2) catalyzes the conversion of arachidonic acid into PGE2 – a pluripotent pro-inflammatory lipid mediator capable of inhibiting TCR-induced T cell activation (Vercammen and Ceuppens, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vercammen and Ceuppens, 1987

claim: Lung, colon and breast cancers are cancer sub-types that overexpress COX-2.
source: In the context of the immune response to cancer, lung, colon and breast cancers are some of the cancer sub-types that overexpress COX-2 (Wang and DuBois, 2008; Nie, 2007; Hosomi et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang and DuBois, 2008; Nie, 2007; Hosomi et al., 2000

claim: High levels of PGE2 produced by COX-2-over-producing cancers contribute substantially to tumor-generated suppression that prevents the immune system from engaging these cancers effectively.
source: The high levels of PGE2 produced by these COX-2-over-producing cancers contribute substantially to the tumor-generated suppression that prevent the immune system from engaging these cancers effectively (Greenhough et al., 2009; Hashemi Goradel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Greenhough et al., 2009; Hashemi Goradel et al., 2019

claim: PGE2-induced activation of HPK1 utilizes PKA to phosphorylate serine 171.
source: However, instead of serine 171 being phosphorylated by PKD, PGE2-induced activation of HPK1 utilizes PKA to phosphorylate serine 171 (Sawasdikosol et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sawasdikosol et al., 2007

claim: PGE2 could activate HPK1 in mutant Jurkat T cells lines that are deficient in either ZAP-70, LAT or SLP-76.
source: PGE2 could activate HPK1 in mutant Jurkat T cells lines that are deficient in either ZAP-70, LAT or SLP-76, suggesting that EP2 and EP4 receptors utilize a distinct signal transduction cascade from that used by the TCR to activate HPK1 (Sawasdikosol et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Sawasdikosol et al., 2007

claim: EP2 and EP4 receptors utilize a distinct signal transduction cascade from that used by the TCR to activate HPK1.
source: PGE2 could activate HPK1 in mutant Jurkat T cells lines that are deficient in either ZAP-70, LAT or SLP-76, suggesting that EP2 and EP4 receptors utilize a distinct signal transduction cascade from that used by the TCR to activate HPK1 (Sawasdikosol et al., 2007).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing PGE2 activation in ZAP-70, LAT, or SLP-76 deficient cells

claim: Upon Fas engagement, the adaptor molecule FADD is recruited to Fas and forms the death-inducing signaling complex with procaspase-8 and procaspase-10.
source: Upon Fas engagement, the adaptor molecule FADD is recruited to Fas and forms the death-inducing signaling complex with procaspase-8 and procaspase-10 (Dickens et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dickens et al., 2012

claim: Activation of the caspase cascade leads to proteolytic cleavage of HPK1 at aspartic acid residue 385, which is located within the DDVD consensus caspase recognition site of HPK1.
source: Activation of this caspase cascade leads to proteolytic cleavage of HPK1 at aspartic acid residue 385, which is located within the DDVD consensus caspase recognition site of HPK1 (Chen et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 1999

claim: Caspase-processed HPK1 forms a 43 kD kinase domain-containing N-terminal fragment and a 54 kD C-terminal fragment containing three proline-rich regions and the citron homology domain.
source: Caspase-processed HPK1 forms a 43 kD kinase domain-containing N-terminal fragment and a 54 kD C-terminal fragment containing three proline-rich regions and the citron homology domain (Chen et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 1999

claim: The cleaved N-terminal kinase domain acquires a more hyperactive and sustained kinase activity than the non-cleaved full length HPK1 while retaining its ability to activate the JNK MAPK pathway.
source: The cleaved N-terminal kinase domain acquires a more hyperactive and sustained kinase activity than the non-cleaved full length HPK1 while retaining its ability to activate the JNK MAPK pathway (Arnold et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arnold et al., 2007

claim: The kinase activity of HPK1 activates the JNK pathway via the activation of the MEKK1/MKK/JNK signaling cascade.
source: The association between HPK1 kinase activity and the activation of JNK MAPK pathway had been previously established (Kiefer et al., 1996; Hu et al., 1996) and ectopic expression studies using dominant interfering mutants that function upstream of JNK in hematopoietic and epithelial cell lines revealed that the kinase activity of HPK1 activate the JNK pathway via the activation of the MEKK1/MKK/JNK signaling cascade (Hu et al., 1996; Chen and Tan, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kiefer et al., 1996; Hu et al., 1996; Chen and Tan, 2000

claim: The three-dimensional structure of HPK1 kinase domain exists as a head-to-head domain-swapped dimer in both the crystal form and in the liquid form.
source: This speculation is strengthened by the recent X-ray crystallographic studies revealing that the three-dimensional structure of HPK1 kinase domain exists as a head-to-head domain-swapped dimer in both the crystal form, as well as in the liquid form Wu et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2019.
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2019

claim: In the non-phosphorylated, inactive state, the activation loop of each HPK1 monomer partially occupies the ATP- and substrate-binding sites of its partner monomer.
source: In the non-phosphorylated, inactive state, the activation loop of each HPK1 monomer partially occupies the ATP- and substrate-binding sites of its partner monomer, thus serving as a possible mechanism to quiesce the basal kinase activity of HPK1.
evidence: Inferred from structural studies

claim: The trans-inhibitory posture of the activation loop is disrupted when threonine residue 165 and serine residue 171 are phosphorylated.
source: This trans-inhibitory posture of the activation loop is disrupted when the threonine residue 165 and serine residue 171 are phosphorylated (Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2019

claim: The proteolytically cleaved 54 kD C-terminal fragment has no catalytic activity but plays an important role in the regulation of apoptosis via its ability to inhibit the NFκB pathway.
source: The proteolytically cleaved 54 kD C-terminal fragment that contains three proline-rich regions and the citron homology domain has no catalytic activity, but plays an important role in the regulation of apoptosis via its ability to inhibit the NFκB pathway (Chen et al., 1999; Arnold et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 1999; Arnold et al., 2001

claim: Full length HPK1 activates the NFκB pathway during the early, non-AICD-sensitive phase of T cell activation through phosphorylation of the linker region of CARMA1 at serine 549 and 551.
source: Full length HPK1 had been shown to activate the NFκB pathway during the early, non-AICD-sensitive phase of T cell activation (Arnold et al., 2001; Brenner et al., 2005), through phosphorylation of the linker region of CARMA1 at serine 549 and 551 (Arnold et al., 2001; Brenner et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arnold et al., 2001; Brenner et al., 2005; Brenner et al., 2009

claim: The phosphorylated CARMA1 complexes with Bcl10 and MALT1 to form the CARMA1/Bcl10/MALT1 complex that phosphorylates and activates IKK kinase activity.
source: The phosphorylated CARMA1 complexes with Bcl10 and MALT1 to form the CARMA1/Bcl10/MALT1 that phosphorylates and activates IKK kinase activity, resulting in IKK degradation and initiation of the NFκB activation cascade (Brenner et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brenner et al., 2009

claim: Once HPK1 is cleaved by caspase, its HPK1-C fragment continues to bind to IKKα and IKKβ and sequester them in the inactive form, preventing the initiation of the NFκB cascade.
source: Once HPK1 is cleaved by caspase, its HPK1-C fragment continues to bind to IKKα and IKKβ and sequester them in the inactive form, preventing the initiation of the NFκB cascade (Brenner et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brenner et al., 2005

claim: NK cells isolated from catalytically inactive K46M HPK1 mutant mice possess increased cytotoxic activity in vitro against YAC-1, a NK-sensitive murine lymphoma, when compared to wild type NK cells.
source: In this regard, NK cells isolated from catalytically inactive K46M HPK1 mutant mice were shown to possess increased cytotoxic activity in vitro against YAC-1, a NK-sensitive murine lymphoma, when compared to the activity of wild type NK cells (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Liu et al., 2019

claim: The loss of HPK1 kinase activity correlates with higher titers of IgG1 and IgG2b produced in response to immunization.
source: While there is no direct evidence to suggest that HPK1 is involved in ADCC, there is evidence that the loss of HPK1 kinase activity correlates with higher titers of IgG1 and IgG2b produced in response to immunization (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019

claim: HPK1-/- bone marrow derived dendritic cells (BMDCs) exhibited elevated levels of CD80 and CD86 in response to LPS stimulation.
source: The first evidence that HPK1 is involved in the second step of cancer-immunity cycle came when it was shown that HPK1-/- bone marrow derived dendritic cells (BMDCs) exhibited elevated levels of CD80 and CD86 in response to receiving maturation signal via LPS stimulation (Alzabin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Alzabin et al., 2009

claim: HPK1-/- BMDCs demonstrated increased levels of IL-12 production, reduced levels of IL-10 and an enhanced ability to present peptide antigen.
source: These HPK1-/- BMDCs also demonstrated increased levels of IL-12 production, reduced levels of IL-10 and an enhanced ability to present peptide antigen.
evidence: Inferred from the description of HPK1-/- BMDC properties

claim: Ovalbumin immunized HPK1-/- BMDCs could elicit a greater proliferative response of adoptively transferred OTI T cells than their wild type counterpart.
source: Ovalbumin immunized HPK1-/- BMDCs could elicit a greater proliferative response of adoptively transferred OTI T cells than their wild type counterpart.
evidence: Inferred from the description of experimental results

claim: Catalytically-inactive K46M HPK1 BMDCs elicit an elevated OTI proliferative response to ovalbumin peptide in vitro.
source: This finding is consistent with the report of an elevated OTI proliferative response to enhanced antigen presentation by ovalbumin peptide-pulsed catalytically-inactive K46M HPK1 BMDCs in vitro, which suggests the enhanced antigen presentation is dependent of the HPK1 kinase activity (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Liu et al., 2019

claim: HPK1-/- BMDCs were resistant to LPS-mediated activation-induced apoptosis.
source: Given that the HPK1-/- BMDCs were resistant to LPS-mediated activation-induced apoptosis and HPK1-/- T cells are also resistant to PGE2-induced apoptosis (Alzabin et al., 2009; Alzabin et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Alzabin et al., 2009; Alzabin et al., 2010

claim: HPK1-/- T cells are resistant to PGE2-induced apoptosis.
source: Given that the HPK1-/- BMDCs were resistant to LPS-mediated activation-induced apoptosis and HPK1-/- T cells are also resistant to PGE2-induced apoptosis (Alzabin et al., 2009; Alzabin et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Alzabin et al., 2009; Alzabin et al., 2010

claim: The ectopic expression of HPK1 in Jurkat T cells reduced TCR-induced Erk MAPK and AP-1 activation while the expression of a catalytically inactivated point mutant form of HPK1 could not.
source: The initial clue that the kinase activity of HPK1 plays a role in inhibiting TCR-induced activation signal came when it was reported that the ectopic expression of HPK1 in Jurkat T cells reduced TCR-induced Erk MAPK and AP-1 activation while the expression of a catalytically inactivated point mutant form of HPK1 could not (Liou et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Liou et al., 2000

claim: Jurkat cells treated with Sunitinib malate (Sutent) could produce more IL-2 in response to TCR engagement, resulting in enhanced phosphorylation of Erk MAPK and elevated IL-2 production.
source: This early finding is consistent with our early observation that Jurkat cells, when treated with Sunitinib malate (Sutent), could produce more IL-2 in response to TCR engagement, resulting in enhanced phosphorylation of Erk MAPK and elevated IL-2 production [unpublished observation and (Johnson et al., 2019)].
evidence: Supported by unpublished observation and citation to Johnson et al., 2019

claim: Sutent is a multi-kinase inhibitor capable of inhibiting HPK1 kinase activity in vitro at an IC50 of 15 nM.
source: Sutent, the multi-kinase inhibitor was capable of inhibiting HPK1 kinase activity in vitro at an IC50 of 15 nM (Anastassiadis et al., 2011; Davis et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anastassiadis et al., 2011; Davis et al., 2011

claim: The loss of HPK1 correlates strongly with heightened level of T cell activation as evidenced by increased proliferation, sustained TCR-induced calcium flux and elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-2, TNF-α and IFN-γ.
source: The loss of HPK1 correlates strongly with the heightened level of T cell activation as evidenced by increased proliferation, sustained TCR-induced calcium flux and elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-2, TNF-α and IFN-γ (Alzabin et al., 2010; Shui et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alzabin et al., 2010; Shui et al., 2007

claim: HPK1-/- mice possess an enhanced immunopathologic response to myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) in a murine experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model.
source: HPK1-/- mice also possess an enhanced immunopathologic response to myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) in a murine experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model (Shui et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Shui et al., 2007

claim: HPK1 expression was reduced in CD4+ T cells of systemic lupus erythematosus patients due to jumonji domain containing 3 (JMJD3)-mediated H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) of the HPK1 promoter.
source: These murine studies were consistent with a report that HPK1 expression was reduced in CD4+ T cells of systemic lupus erythematosus patients due to jumonji domain containing 3 (JMJD3)-mediated H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) of the HPK1 promoter (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2011

claim: A reduction of HPK1 expression was detected by microarray analysis of RNA prepared from PBMC of psoriatic arthritis patients.
source: A similar report of the reduction of HPK1 expression was detected by microarray analysis of RNA prepared from PBMC of psoriatic arthritis patients (Batliwalla et al., 2005; Stoeckman et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Batliwalla et al., 2005; Stoeckman et al., 2006

claim: Adoptive transfer of HPK1-/- T cells is sufficient to confer host mice with the ability to reject the 3LL lung carcinoma.

claim: T cells from both K46E and K46M mutant mice failed to phosphorylate SLP-76 at serine 376 and responded to TCR engagement with elevated activation of the Erk MAPK pathway and higher levels of IL-2 and IFN-γ production compared to wild type T cells.
source: T cells from both the K46E and K46M mutant mice failed to phosphorylate SLP-76 at serine 376 and responded to TCR engagement with elevated activation of the Erk MAPK pathway and coincided with higher levels of IL-2 and IFN-γ production when compared to wild type T cells.
